props.title: The Missionary

sections.content: **The Missionary** (1982) represents a fascinating intersection of Monty Python-adjacent comedy and period drama, starring Python alumnus Michael Palin in a surprisingly nuanced performance. The film follows Reverend Charles Fortescue's return from Africa to establish a mission for London's "fallen women," blending British social commentary with subtle humor. Like A Private Function (1984) and Time Bandits (1981), it showcases Palin's ability to carry a film beyond pure comedy into more complex dramatic territory. HandMade Films, George Harrison's production company, continued their streak of unique British productions here, following their success with **Life of Brian** (1979).

sections.content: The film's examination of Victorian social hypocrisy shares DNA with more serious period pieces like **The French Lieutenant's Woman** (1981) and later works such as **Angels and Insects** (1995). Director Richard Loncraine brings a measured touch that distinguishes **The Missionary** from broader religious satires like **Nuns on the Run** (1990), instead focusing on character-driven humor and social observation. Maggie Smith's performance as Lady Isabel Ames adds layers of complexity to what could have been a one-note aristocratic character. SUBHEAD: British Comedy Evolution

**The Missionary** marks an important transition in British comedy cinema of the 1980s, moving away from the anarchic style of the 1970s toward more sophisticated narrative structures. This shift can be traced through films like **Educating Rita** (1983) and **Local Hero** (1983), where comedy serves character development rather than mere punchlines. The film's treatment of religion and sexuality, while tame by modern standards, was notably progressive for its time, predating similar themes in **Scandal** (1989) and **Prick Up Your Ears** (1987).
